subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the few changes in the tariff which are indicated in this budget are of a character which will give satisfaction to the interests concerned in the district which I represent. The principal ones are those dealing with coal. It so happen!; that both the increase and the decrease indicated by the budget will be of benefit to the mines in my district. These mines, as the House generally knows, are in a very desperate condition owing to the competition of fuel oil, and our principal market is in the United States. There is a reciprocal item in the United States tariff by which the duty on Canadian coal going into the United States rises or falls in the same way as our duty on American coal coming into Canada. Consequently, the reduction of duty on bituminous coal from 53 to 50 cents a ton will be of advantage to us in the American market. Three cents is not a very big reduction and it might well have been more. It amounts to only six per cent, but six per cent of a reduction in the tariff is always better than nothing. On the other hand, the increase in the duty on slack coal also benefits us because we have practically no market for slack coal, in the United States. We produce very little of it in any case, and a considerable trade has been growing up of late years in slack coal coming from the United States into Vancouver. I judge from the change in the tariff that this will be entirely done away with.
There is a matter in connection with lignite that I should like to draw to the attention of the government. I have done so already, but I want to impress it upon them once more. Some years ago the government made a change in the duty on lignite, putting it on the free list in order to facilitate the sale of coal from southern Alberta into the United States. At that time there was no influx of lignite from the United States into Canada on the Pacific coast. Lignite and bituminous are more or less comparative terms. You cannot say precisely by looking at coal that this particular coal is lignite and that bituminous. The question is one of analysis, and the Customs department, in order to arrive at some basis on which to gauge the entry of this coal, agreed between the two nations that if coal went over six per cent of moisture, it would be considered as lignite. The result of that ruling was that there started up a trade in lignite coal going into Vancouver from the Bellingham mines in the state of Washington to the south, a trade that had never been thought of or contemplated, before. The coal for that purpose was analysed and it went 6.1 per cent of moisture, or just one-

The Budget-Mr. Neill
tenth of one per cent over the amount at which it would be allowed in free. At my suggestion last year the government had it analyzed again and it came to 6.7 per cent of moisture, bringing it apparently well into the lignite class. I submit, .however, it is not lignite and should not be so classified. I have in my hand a bulletin of the Washington Department of Conservation and Development in which they deal with these Bellingham coals and they distinctly say:
It is often referred to as lignite, but more properly it should be classed as a low grade bituminous coal.

speechtext: What is the percentage of carbon in the coal?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I have here an analysis, but it is defined merely as moisture, ash, F.C.- whatever that stands for,-and B.T.U.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
It does not give the carbon apparently, but the moisture,content; the bulletin gives its moisture as well below six per cent, so that, in the opinion of the Washington Department of Conservation and Development, the coal should be classified, not as lignite, but as low-grade bituminous. Yet we are allowing it to come in as a lignite coal. I have also in my hand a statement showing the quantities that have come in. In 1923, the quantity of lignite coal that came into British Columbia from the United States was 2,331 tons and, in 1924, the trade had grown, owing to this favourable tariff regulation, to 25,763 tons. On the other hand, the benefit that we looked for has not taken place. The quantity of lignite coal going out of Alberta into the United States in 1923 was over 21,000 tons and, in 1924, it was only 12,302 tons. Therefore, for the sake of getting a sale of 12,000 tons of lignite from Alberta, we are sacrificing the British Columbia coal industry to the extent of 25,763 tons of lignite coming in from \V a^iington. And when I point out, as I have, that this is not really lignite but low-grade bituminous, I think it will be very proper for the government to raise the point of analysis from 6 per cent to 7 per cent moisture. That would cut out the imported coal coming into Vancouver and possibly prevent some of the lignite coal going from Alberta. But even if it did prevent it all it would be better to do so than to build up a trade which would be more antagonistic to British Columbia than beneficial to Alberta.
Turning now to another item of the budget, I would deal for a moment with the reduction of the duty on engines used in the pro-112i
pulsion of fishing boats. This is something that will be very acceptable to the fishing population of the Pacific, and no doubt to those on the Atlantic. The previous tax was 15 per cent on engines of British origin and 27| per cent on those coming from the United States, and that has been cut down to 10 per cent and 15 per cent respectively. Coupled with the reduction in the sales tax last year, this represents a substantial saving to those who buy these engines. Taking the average price of one of these fishing boat engines, which probably would be $160, the total reduction in the duty now would represent a saving of something like $35.50 on each engine which is a substantial amount to a poor man buying an engine for his own use. I am also pleased to see the way in which these engines are now exempted from the sales tax. Last year the exemption provision read, "Gasoline engines to be used in boats, etc.", and that has been struck out now and the provision stated in a different form referring to item 453e. Hon. gentlemen will appreciate the significance of this when I say that many fishing boat engines do not use gasoline but distillate and coal oil. Diesel and semi-Diesel engines are coming into use now and they are using a low grade of crude oil, and under the change I Have indicated it will enable the sales tax to be taken off all these engines which are used for practically the same purpose. Heretofore they were not eligible under this class inasmuch as they did not use gasoline. These are practically all the tariff changes that affect my district.
I have been asked by a body of my constituents to urge upon the government the raising of the duty on eggs from 3 cents to 8 cents in order to make the Canadian duty equal to that imposed by our American friends.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I thought that would raise applause from my right. Well, that brings up the whole question of tariff on the one hand and low tariff on the other.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Does not the hon. member's judgment warrant his urging upon the government personally such an increase?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
If the hon. member will wait a little I will reveal what my judgment is in the matter. As I -was saying, this opens up the whole question of tariff and low tariff. I have sat in this House for four years and I will undertake to say that sixty per cent of that time has been spent by members on both sides in an utterly fruitless, useless,
The Budget-Mr. Neill

unnecessary attempt to convince the other part of the House as to the merits of the tariff question. I do not propose to be led down that enticing but bewildering vista; I decline to be drawn into it. Our friends to the right, as they have just indicated, will applaud this request that I have just brought to the attention of the House, in the conviction that it will increase the price of eggs to the producer in British Columbia. On the other hand, no doubt, the low tariff men would say that an increase of that kind would raise the cost of living and also probably result in a reduced demand, and that in the case of an article of such common and universal use it would only require the individual householder to make a small restriction in their use to materially affect the demand, so that the reduced demand would so bring down the price that possibly the result would be no better than if the tariff had been left alone. I will leave the subject in that way without expressing any opinion. But I will say this, that the situation as regards the importation of eggs has been materially improved in the last few years. When this government came into power they found some measure of egg inspection but it was of such a weird character as to prove futile against the importer of foreign eggs, while it was a real 'nuisance to what we may call the domestic importer, that is to say, the person importing from one province to another. The government changed that system to make it apply to the importer of foreign eggs, whether from China or from the United States. I recall the investigations that took place at that time, when there was an enormous influx of Chinese eggs. I remember one shipment alone of 50,000 cases which were traced to Montreal and some to Ottawa. Since then, owing to the rigid enforcement of the system of inspection, the situation has greatly improved, and although it is a source of annoyance to some country storekeepers, the results in the main have been beneficial. In the first two years since the inspection system has been applied the importation of Chinese eggs in 1923-24 was absolutely nil. In this last year there has been an importation of some 75,000 dozen, of which 30,000 have been rejected. This will help to discourage their entrance and will also, I hope, tend to keep up the quality. As regards the importation of eggs from the American side, the figures are also son ewhat encouraging. In the year 1923 the importation of eggs in dozens from the United States was 8,256.000 and in the following year 6,454,000 while in the year ending March 23 last, only a week short of the year, 
the importation was only 2,429,000. It is apparent, therefore, that instead of becoming more acute the situation is rather improved. Now, for the consolation of my friends who can see only through one glass, namely protection, I would suggest another method of assisting our egg producers in British Columbia-and I know that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) will be peculiarly interested in the fortunes of egg producers seeing that he represents a city constituency. Here is -what I suggest as something that would materially help the situation. When the government bring down their policy in connection with the regulation of freight rates, if they will see to it that the exceedingly unjust discrimination that exists to-day in the freight on wheat from the prairies is done away with, it will be of great benefit to egg producers. When a farmer in the prairies ships No. 1 wheat, worth probably $2, to Vancouver and it is going to China or to Great Britain, he pays a rate on it of 22J cents a hundred, but if the same farmer ships No. 6 wheat which is worth perhaps only $1 he pays, or the consumer in British Columbia pays, a rate of 414 cents. Now, if there is any possible way of justifying such a discrimination I should like to hear it, for I have not found anyone who is prepared to defend it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: It exists elsewhere; the same discrimination exists in shipments from Winnipeg to Fort William.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
If the hon. member is prepared to sit down and see that injustice continue in Manitoba that is no reason why we should have it in British Columbia. I was pointing out that there is a discrimination of $3.80 a ton or $133 a carload, and it is claimed by the British Columbia Poultry Exchange- whose membership I do not know, although I know that it does not embrace all British Columbia-that there is a loss of $75,000 a year in connection with this one item alone. If the railways can carry 20,000 carloacfs of wheat at 21 cents per hundred-and I do not think it is denied that they carry it at a profit -surely they can carry 2.000 more at the same rate for local consumption in British Columbia, and so for once place the British Columbia farmer on a par at least with his Japanese and Chinese competitors or with the consumer in Britain. For it is when the wheat is exported, no matter where it goes, that the low rate applies; when it is used in British Columbia the high rate must be paid. If the government can adjust this matter it will be doing a lot for the egg producers of British Columbia, and it would not involve

The Budget-Mr. Neill
any tariff alterations. Certainly the present injustice, which cannot for a moment be defended, should be done away with.
There is another matter affecting British Columbia. I refer to the protection of the west coast,-I am not now talking about naval defence, but about protection against shipwreck and the like. I wish to congratulate very heartily the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) for the success of the development on the west coast of the direction-finding apparatus that he installed there some years ago. It is located at a point called Pachena. It was very carefully located, the men in charge are thoroughly efficient, and the apparatus appears to be of the very finest. The files of the government offices are full of letters of warm thanks from captains and shipping companies for the benefits they have secured from being able to receive the location of their ships by means of this apparatus, because the west coast where the station is located is a place where it is peculiarly easy for ships to go wrong; the currents are rather variable, at a certain point -navigators have to make a sharp turn to get into the straits, and at night time or in foggy or dull weather they are very liable to overrun their reckoning and be on the shores of Vancouver island before they know it. During the past winter there has not been a single wreck on that coast, which in itself is a tribute to the efficiency of the installation and to the efficiency of those in charge of it. I think it was last year that the Americans, who maintain two or three similar stations along their coast line, initiated a competition to see-which station would be most accurate in giving locations of vessels, and they warned their own stations that they were going to have this contest, but they did not warn the Pachena station, although they took it into the competition. In the result the Pachena station beat all the American stations in accuracy. I think its fraction of error was only something like three per cent over a long series of contests. That alone, I think, is a striking tribute to the efficiency of our Canadian staff.
In this connection there is another matter which I should mention, in the hope of obtaining further action. A couple of years ago the Minister of Marine and Fisheries installed at Bamfield for the four winter months a boat equipped with wireless that would be always available with steam up to go to the succour of any vessels in distress. It was an excellent idea and saved both shipping and human life. But the best boat available was one of the fishery patrol boats, and while, as I say, it did good work on several occasions, yet emergencies might easily have arisen to cope with
which that boat would have been absolutely useless, its insufficient breadth of beam and lack of power rendering it unsuitable for such operations. But still we were glad to get that boat. Now the government have for some years been subsidizing to a considerable amount a salvage company which keeps a salvage boat always under steam at Esquimalt in the vicinity of Victoria. But 'Esquimalt is too far away from the west coast; it is like having a fire apparatus for Ottawa stationed twenty miles out in the country. This company has had built at enormous expense a very fine type of boat; indeed it is the very last word in improvements for succouring boats in distress. That boat has been brought out to Victoria. Now, I would suggest that the government should pay the company a slightly larger subsidy for the purpose of having that improved boat kept at Bamfield during the four winter months, for there it would be of the very greatest service to west coast shipping. This boat is even superior to the American boat Snohomish which has been maintained for the same purpose by the United States authorities, and has long been our envy and admiration. It would be an inestimable boon to the west coast if the minister could see his way to give a little extra subsidy and have the boat stationed at Bamfield. Then it could be said indeed that we had a first class wreck protection service on the west coast.
Another item I would call to the attention of the government is in connection with our soldier settlers. The committee that reported on this last session recommended that there should be a flat reduction of sixty per cent and forty per cent on the stock purchased by these settlers in certain years. That portion of the report was concurred in by the House and by the minister, who specifically stated that he approved the proposal. I trust that that recommendation will be carried out. It is a good one, because we are all aware that the stock was purchased at too dear a price at that time and it would be no use trying to have a revaluation of it ito-day. Therefore a flat rate would be perfectly equitable to all and sundry, and I hope the government will carry out the recommendation this year. In fact they are almost pledged to do so. The other feature has to do with revaluation of the land. The committee's recommendation on this subject was left in abeyance, not being concurred in bv the House, but the minister assured us it was going to receive his consideration during the recess. Now, a flat rate of reduction on the value of all these lands would be absolutely useless, indeed I think it would be positively wrong, for this reason: There are a large number of farms on which no
The Budget-Mr. Neill

rebate is required at all; if they were revalued they would probably show a value higher than when bought. To give a flat rebate, it would have to be necessarily very small, perhaps ten per cent, which would be absurd, for it would be giving ito a large number of soldier settlers something they do not require, and on the other hand it would be denying 'justice to a number of other settlers who need assistance very badly. An average rebate of ten per cent would be of no use at all to this latter class, whereas if the rebate was confined only to those soldiers applying for it, of course they would not seek it if they thought the valuation of their property would be raised, and so the government could afford to give a reasonable rebate to those whose land was undoubtedly purchased at too high a price. When the Prime Minister and his party were in British Columbia last summer they did the Comox-Albemi district the honour of visiting it. We were very proud to see him and his party, and he was kind enough to give an interview to a deputation of these soldier settlers, and he was further good enough to go out and see for himself some of the uncleared bush land from which had been taken all the merchantable timber, leaving stumps running perhaps twenty or thirty to the acre and from three to four feet through, and which could not be cleared at less than $10 to $15 apiece; and in some cases the second growth has covered the land. The Prime Minister was told that that land was bought for the soldiers in the early days of their return at $45 an acre, but the current value of similar land alongside, both then and now, was between $5 and S7.50 per acre. It matters not now whether there was graft or mere mismanagement; there was a rush in those early days, and something had to be done in a hurry. Here is a case where an investigation should take place, and these men should get a substantial reduction on the original cost of their land. It may be asked: What is the use of always asking the government to spend money and then passing resolutions denouncing them for it. But this is not a case of spending money at all; it is a case of throwing out these people and then taking in others to fill their place to whom you will have to sell the land, not at the original price but at its present value. The original purchase money is gone; it was gone when whoever was in charge bought this land at six times what it was worth. It is now a question whether you are to throw out these soldier settlers and sell their land to other people-perhaps orientals-at its present value, and take the loss; or let these men stay on the land at its present value and (Mr. Neill.]
take the loss; the loss will have to be taken in any case. I would suggest therefore that it would be a very proper thing indeed for the government to go very thoroughly into this subject and have a revaluation of all the soldiers' land where required.
There is' another matter I would like to touch on, and that is the question of old age pensions. I was very much pleased to see the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) give notice that a committee would be re-appointed this year to deal with this matter. I trust that the personnel will be the same as that of last year, because we understand the subject and are in a position to deal with it easier than it can be dealt with by others starting afresh. The resolution that that committee brought down last year was a recommendation to the government to devise a scheme on a very modest scale of old age pensions, with the understanding that each province that wished to take it up would pay half the cost. The idea was that the provinces are now compelled to meet the whole cost of aid to destitute people, and although under the new plan they would pay half of the larger sum involved, they would probably pay no more in the long run than they are paying now, and the pension system would be a suitable one to all concerned. The question of destitute relief is getting acute in some of the provinces and this would be a method of dealing with it. I understand that the government consulted the provinces in the recess to find out what their attitude was, and I suppose the answer of the provinces will be submitted to this committee and I hope we will be able to arrive at some conclusion and make some recommendation to the government by which this question may be dealt with. It is an all-important matter; it is a phase of social reform in Canada that should be brought more to the front in the political programme of both parties in the near future.
Having talked to-day and last night for an hour and a half without mentioning the oriental question perhaps I may be permitted to refer to it now. I do not intend to discuss the principle involved; I consider that that was well defined in the resolution passed by this House in May, 1922. Public sentiment since then has crystallized into the belief that that resolution expresses the situation, not only as it was but also as it should be, in regard to governmental action. It is very brief; I will quote it for the sake of getting it on Hansard:
That, in the opinion of this House, the immigration of oriental aliens and their rapid multiplication is becoming a serious menace to living conditions, particularly on the Pacific coast, and to the future of the

The Budget-Mr. Neill
country in general, and the government should take immediate action with a view to securing the exclusion of future immigration of this type.
It was moved by a member of the government that the word "exclusion" be struck out and the words "effective restriction" be substituted therefor, which was done. But it was done with the assurance of several members of the cabinet that the words "effective restriction" would be held to mean, although for diplomatic reasons the idea was otherwise expressed, the same as exclusion. That was the resolution that was passed at that time, and it was strengthened by the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the debate on July 11, last year, in which he used this language-I will quote only one sentence:
If we find that we cannot get effective restriction in the manner I have described, the government will be prepared to consider any further restrictive measure which my hon. friend or his friends from British Columbia may bring to its attention.
Now, I wish to deal wdth the situation since, starting, as it were, from that resolution; with what has been done by the government to implement that resolution and that pledge, and what yet remains to be done. The government have done three things, which I will deal with individually, In the first place they passed the Chinese Immigration Act, which to my mind has been an unqualified success. I asked for returns the other day and I find that in the calendar year past practically no Chinese immigrants have come to Canada: only two members of the diplomatic service, two of their servants, no merchants, no students. Seventy-four came in under permit, which means that they may stay not longer than six months. Out of the seventy-four, thirty-five were Chinese actors under permit, and these were compelled to put up bonds to ensure their going out within the specified time. The rest of those who came under permit were of the classes that none could take exception to- clergymen and their wives, consular service and immigration agents; Chinese passenger agents, and so on. So it may well be held that this act has dealt effectively with the exclusion demand so far as the Chinese are concerned. I may say, too, that much of the success of it was due to the efficient manner in which the immigration officers administered the act. I have been to some trouble to check them up; I cross-examined them, almost, in the matter, and I am well satisfied that they are enforcing the act very rigidly, but still in a fair and reasonable spirit. I think it may also be said that the results in a political sense are highly satisfactory. There was a little friction at the time with the Chinese, but that has died out and I firmly believe there is a better feeling between Chinese and the white men in British Columbia than there ever was before. The Chinese know just exactly where they are, and what their limitations are. The white man, when he is brought in contact with the Chinaman by competition, is able to say: "Well, you are there, but no more of you will come in," and he is satisfied, so to speak, to leave the Chinaman where he is. So much for that phase of it.
Then, the second thing that the government have done in fulfilment of this pledge is to place restrictions upon orientals in the fishing industry. This is a subject that requires a little consideration. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Fournier), I think, was speaking somewhere in Ontario the other day, and I saw in the paper that he made the comment that it was noticeable how the habit of " propagandering ", if that is the right word, has increased since the -war. We learned it during the war days, and, as he pointed out, every big industry, almost every large organization, now maintains a press agent for the purpose of disseminating propaganda. I had noticed that myself, and' I look upon it as a regrettable thing. I think it was much better in the old days when news *was collected by reporters, employees of the press. They were reliable, intelligent and unprejudiced men, and what they collected and prepared for publication was generally pretty nearly accurate. If it was left to them to-day it would be the same thing. But now the press agent sits in his office and writes out a dozen, yes, two or three dozen, little news items, varying them a little from time to time, and he sends a few of them out to this paper or that magazine at the last minute. The editor has usually no reason to suspect there is anything wrong with them. Perhaps the main idea of the article or news item is true, but it is skilfully perverted to educate the public along one particular line and to convince them that something is true which is not true-because that is the main idea of propaganda. Now, that has been done in this matter. There has been a very skilful and, I should imagine,

I hope so at any rate-well-paid propaganda in connection with these restrictions upon orientals in the fishing industry in British Columbia. It has been widespread; letters and telegrams have poured in to the minister, some from this angle, some from that angle, in order to concentrate upon him and to give the impression that there is a general feeling
The Budget-Mr. Neill

in British Columbia in connection with this matter. The idea is to show that the whole thing was a mistake; that it had misfired and should be corrected. But this is all propaganda; it is "bunk" of the plainest description. Any man with a printed letterhead that did not too plainly betray his connection with the Japanese, and who was unpatriotic enough to do it, was invited to write to the minister expressing his views. I traced some of these to their source and in almost every case I found that if they were not in the direct pay of the Japanese they were obliged to them in matters of business relations, and so on. There was another feature I noticed, too, in this white propaganda, so to speak: it was how wild their remarks were; how inaccurate their statements. The Japanese put in petitions of their own, but at least they knew what they were talking about and kept within the bounds of moderation in their arguments. But these men who did not know the first thing they were talking about simply let themselves go to please their oriental allies and made some of the most ridiculous statements you could imagine. The press was not lost sight of, either. Little news items were sent to this newspaper and to that; or articles occasionally appeared.' They were usually, however, in the form of letters to the editor, signed by "Tom Smith" or "Bill Jones". I was particularly impressed by one contributor *-I forget his name-who, in order to make good his case and to earn his money, in the course of a violent attack upon myself made the statement that he was able to produce individual Japanese who had done more for the progress and prosperity of British Columbia than the whole tribe of Neills from creation down. Mr. Speaker, I would like if I had time to get in touch with that gentleman. I admire the research he must have made to trace my pedigree back as far as that. So far as my family records go, I can only go back a couple of hundred years, when one of, my ancestors met a violent death. The democratic wing of our family says that he was hanged for sheep stealing, but the more aristocratic members claim that he was beheaded for intrusion into the politics of the day. We all know that at that time it was quite an honourable thing for a worn out politician to be beheaded; they had not discovered the Senate in those days!
I would like to point out, in justice to mj^self and also to other members, that this restriction on Japanese fishing in British Columbia is not the work of one member, or of two or three members, at all. and it did not originate entirely in British Columbia.
'Mr Neill.]
It was the recommendation of a commission -I have its report here, but I shall not read it

a commission composed of six members of parliament, of all political parties. Two of them came from the east, and so were quite untrammelled by our local prejudices; they saw things for themselves. And the resolution recommending this restriction was passed unanimously by the commission. Further than that-the members who came from the east are in the House and can bear me out- the conditions so surprised them, hit them so much harder than us who were used to them, that when we came to consider the restriction clause they were prepared to go much further than we were. They were prepared to make it a whole sweep of one hundred per cent, but we, knowing the local conditions, said: " No, let us go slow, and then we are likely to go further." But certainly that recommendation was not the idea simply of one or two members from British Columbia.
Now the only support of any importance, the only reputable support that this propaganda has received from what I might call any semi-public body, has come from the Canners' Association of British Columbia, and curiously enough, theirs is the only industry in British Columbia that has not suffered from direct competition with the Japanese. I hey have suffered from competition in London, because there the Japanese from Siberia compete with them with Siberia-put-up salmon; but the Japanese have no canneries in British Columbia, and so the British Columbia canners do not suffer from their competition there. There is no other class or industry in British Columbia that does not so suffer. The farms, the logging camps, the mines, even the stores and hotels, every class of industry in British Columbia, suffers from the direct competition of the Japanese, except the canning industry, and the canning industry is the only one demanding that this restriction be taken off the employment of Japanese. And they do not only ask it, they demand it, and they are emphatic in their demands. They go so far as to say: If this is not done, we shall have to shut down;-and when an industry with a capital of $11,000,000 invested in it uses language of that kind we can only conclude either one of two things, either that a really desperate situation exists which deserves investigation, or that some one is putting up a bluff on the people of Canada. Let us consider which of the two it is, for that point is worthy of consideration.
This commission to which I have made reference did not deal harshly with the cannery

The Budget*-Mr. Neill
men of British Columbia by any means. They recognized that they might be put to some loss, or to some inconvenience at least, by this restriction on Japanese, and they considered this in making their recommendations. For that and other reasons they made recommendations that there should be a material reduction in the taxes paid by the canners. The tax on purse-seines used to be S300; the tax on drag-seines at that time was $150; and the government's license on canneries was $500. The commission recommended that all these taxes be brought down to $20 each, and they were all so reduced. The government carried out our recommendation in that respect. Further than that, the commission recommended that the tax of one-half of one cent on each salmon caught in drag-seines, purse-seines and traps be abolished. You can imagine that with the enormous amount of salmon caught, a tax of even half a cent on each individual salmon would amount to a very big sum. The commission recommended that that tax be done away with, and that was done. So the commission did not deal harshly with the canning interests on that occasion.
Now let us deal with the results-not nebulous statements by people who do not know anything about the situation, vague statements that it is going to kill the industry, but cold, hard facts collected from the government returns, not prepared at my suggestion, but issued in the regular way.
I have here a statement of the total pack for the last four years:
Total Pack in Cases
1921		 603,548
1922		 1,290,316
1923		 1,341,677
1924		 1,745,313
This reveals the fact that the 1924 pack of canned salmon in cases was the largest of any year in the history of the industry, even larger than in the bumper year of 1919, just after the war, and which bumper pack was the result of a tremendous effort to stimulate production, and when everything that had a tail that could wiggle or a fin that could shake was jammed into a can and sold. Last year the output was greater than in any previous year. It was 30 per cent greater than in the previous year, it was 36 per cent greater than in 1922, and it rvas S7 per cent greater than in 1921. There is the record of this industry for the last four years-30 per 4 p.m. cent, 36 per cent, and 87 per cent greater than in 1921. You might say: Well, you might catch a lot of fish, and
the more you catch the more you lose. I have heard that statement made by the cannery men.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Was 1921 supposed to be the big year?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
No, 1919. Here is an extract from a trade paper, the Pacific Coast Fisherman, dealing with the British Columbia salmon market. It is taken from its March issue this year.
The British Columbia market continues in very satisfactory shape. Bookings of new-pack sockeyes for Great Britain are already reported at between 75,000 and 80,000 cases, at $14 per case for Skeena and $15 for Fraser river goods; and the tendency of values is strongly upward.
These sales of new-pack sockeyes mean that they are contracting to-day, in March, for delivery of salmon that are still in the water, aind that will not be taken out of the water for four or five months yet, and that will not be on the market for eight or nine months to come. Yet they have already sold 80.000 cases, at a good price, and the prices are tending strongly upward. I go on with the statement:
The only danger seems to be that prices will be advanced too far above the level of Siberian goods, which would invite more competition from the latter. New-pack Pinks also are receiving considerable attention.
Now listen to this:
The only 1924 pack stocks remaining in first hands in the province are Chums, of which there are about 50.000 cases in strong hands. These are firmly held at about $4.25 per case.
I want the House to note that. Out of a total pack of 1,745,000 odd cases, only 50,000 remain in their hands at this season of the year, or less than three per cent. I have often known the canners to be obliged to go on packing their new pack with more than half of the old pack still on their hands; but here we find a situation entirely different. With a pack 87 per cent greater than it was three years ago; with a better price, a cleaned-up market, and selling already a considerable portion of next year's crop; with less overhead,-because, mind you, their contention is that with the lack of Japanese they could not get enough fishermen-and with the cannery license reduced, with the seine license reduced, and with the tax on salmon caught in purse seines abolished; with the industry in that condition they say: " Give us Japs or give us ruin."
Now the argument they use is that white men have not come into the industry in the same proportion as the Japanese went out- that is their whole argument-and that they have consequently suffered from the lack of efficient fishermen.
The Budget-Mr. Neill

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Has the hon. member ever seen an advertisement in any of the newspapers asking for white fishermen?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Never, and to tell the truth, I never expect to, and I see all the coast papers. Let me quote one of the subtle little news items:	,
Statistics show-
They are given to making statements they cannot bear out.
Statistics show that notwithstanding the heavy reduction-
These people have not signed this. It is just a news item and is all part of the propaganda-
-in the number of Japanese licenses in the past three years the number of licenses to white men and Indians has increased only eighteen per cent.
The Japanese reduction was forty per cent.
Canners claim that any further reductions in Japanese fishermen would compel them to apply for the privilege of using traps or to go out of business.
Let us examine that. I will quote some more government statistics. I have before me a statement prepared by the department in the usual course, of licenses issued in 1922 and 1924, before the forty per cent cut came in, and after. It shows the number of licenses issued to Japs in 1922 was 2,933; the number issued in 1924 was 2,241. Deducting the one from the other shows a reduction of 692 licenses in the two years. The number of licenses issued to w'hites and Indians in 1922 was 4,660, I am quite satisfied in including the two together, for the Indians have as much right to employment as we have, they are good citizens and spend their money where they earn it. I have in my hand a notice issued from Tokyo, Japan, which reads as follows:
Remittances home by Japanese working abroad are an appreciable offset to the country's adverse trade balance for the year 1924. For eleven months these have amounted to 33,800,000 yen.
Adding on the proportion for the odd month it comes to nearly twenty million dollars that goes home to Japan every year. I am justified in including the white men and the Indians in the same category.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Is that all from Canada?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
No, it does not say what
amount is from Canada. It is from all different places. The number of white men and Indians who got licenses in 1922 was 4,660, and the number in 1924 was 6,402, showing an increase of 1,742. The total number of licenses

issued to everybody, whites, Indians and Japs, in 1922 was 7,593. The number issued in 1924 was 8,643, or an increase in the total of 1,050.
I want to explain a point there. While I have been adhering to the numbers given here I have been more than fair. People say a man can twist figures to suit himself, but I do not need to do that, because I have a strong case wdthout doing so, and I could use the actual figures and make a much stronger case than I am making, because no one who has not the local knowledge would be able to analyse the figures. But I have taken 468 off the 1924 licenses, because they referred to cod hook and line and grey fish fishing; they were not licensed in 1982 and they were licensed in 1924; therefore if I included them I would be giving an unfair advantage to my own case, so that I do not include them. The net result which I wish to show i3 that the total number of licenses in these two years increased-not decreased-1,050.	Thi
whites and Indians increased 1,742, while the Japs only decreased 692. Surely that does away with the argument that they are being handicapped by the redaction in the Japanese licenses, because they cannot get others to take their place, when not only have the total number increased, but the white men and Indians have increased to the number of 1,742, as against the Jap reduction of 692. But I have Pther figures here going into more detail.
The way the canners do their figuring is this: they take some isolated inlet, and show a reduction there and build up their argument, I am going to show the fallacy of that. Here is one district up north. The total numbei of licenses issued in that district has decreased 14.8, practically fifteen per cent. I admit that That is what they build their argument on They say the white men have not come in, to replace the Japanese. Not only did the white men not increase in that place but they went down thirty-eight per cent. The cut in the Japs in that place was forty per cent. But this return shows that the reduction of Japanese licenses was practically fifty per cent The reason is due to some local condition. Perhaps the salmon did not run that year, or a cannery was shut down. But the whole thing was reduced. If they had been short of men they would have employed their whole quota of Japs, but here they have not employed their whole quota, because the reduction is fifty per cent instead of forty. Here is the district in which they say the white man is going down. Certainly he is going down, because the law of supply and demand enters into it. Here is another case which was featured to the Minister of Marine and

The Budget-Mr. Neill
Fisheries. Take the district of Skeena. In that district they show the licenses had gone down 150, practically fifteen per cent. The number of licenses issued to white men last year in the Skeena was 248, which is an increase of fifty-six per cent. The Indian licenses increased six per cent and the Jap licenses went down forty per cent. The white man goes up fifty-six per cent, the Indian six per cent, the Jap goes down forty per cent and the question is asked, how could there be a reduction in the total? The reason i3 that the Japs outnumbered the white men in that district four to one, and that forty per cent reduction of the Japs came to more than fifty-six per cent increase of the white men. But in an industry where the wdiite men increased fifty-six per cent in two years, surely it cannot be said the white man is not coming in to take the place of the Jap.
There is .another reason I want to give why that reduction occurs, on the top of the reason I have given. That 1922 commission went all over the province and amongst other places we visited Skeena, and there the cannery men and managers came before us and said "We have too many boats on the Skeena". I must say that the cannery men almost entirely provide the gear, the boats, and some expensive nets and give them to fishermen, on shares, and the outlay is considerable. They said, "There are something like 1,100 boats and licenses on t'he river. That number is too many. We would like to go back to the old system of the exclusive privilege where the waters were allocated to the different canneries and each cannery got so many boat licenses." But the late government changed that policy, and this commission could not see their way to do anything different. However, by cutting down the number of Japs we did decrease the number of licenses on that river. The number went down from 1,100 to about 800, and what was the result? The result was that they caught more salmon with a fewer number of boats and with a largely decreased overhead expense. They found they had had too many boats and too much expense. The ruling of the commission in regard to the restriction in the Jap licenses was a perfect God-send to the canners because it enabled them to do what business jealousies had prevented them doing before. Formerly they would not cut down their overhead expenses; they all knew they had too many boats, but one man would not cut down the number of his boats for fear another man might perhaps catch a few fish more than he had. They would not stand for that. The result was that .they kept on this competition until they were on the verge of ruin. They found this was the case and this
reduction was satisfactory as they caught more .salmon at a smaller overhead cost.
But what happened in the next year? The reduction of 40 per cent was in 1923. There was no' reduction in the number of Japs in 1924. So, in 1924 the .cannery men got together and they said: "We have had an object lesson. This thing can be extended. We will agree to cut down the white licenses now because we have still too many." They made what is called a gentleman's agreement amongst themselves, and they cut down the number of boats which they would take at each cannery with the result that they still caught as many fish but naturally they did not employ as many white people. I vrant to quote just a sentence from two or three letters I have here on this subject. This is one from an Old Country fisherman, just out from the Old Country, who went around trying to find employment. I do not know him and will not vouch for him. He wrote to the Vancouver papers complaining of his troubles. I will quote only his last sentence which is this:
However, it is no business of mine to argue the matter, but I would like to question Mr. Rhodes' statement that there are no white men to take up the vacated licenses of the Japs.
Can he tell me why, to all my applications for a net at the different cannery offices in Vancouver, I have received the same reply as I did last year. Full up?
This is another letter from a man I can vouch for, a returned soldier. I know him well and his word is reliable. I quote this from his letter:
I wanted also to state that I was turned down cold at Rivers inlet for a fishing gear. My reason for telling you is because I have heard that there is some fool talk about Japs coming in as of old, on account of a shortage of white men. I happen to be only one of the white men who were refused this past year. British Columbia Packers, Bell Irving and Gosse Millard canneries are the ones I tried. That includes five canneries on Rivers inlet. That was as many as I thought likely and had been told by different parties the others were full up. If I had been a green hand I wouldn't have minded so very much, but I have fished on River's inlet since 1919 and also before I was in the army. Being a British subject is the biggest farce ever pulled as far as fishing goes.
This is the complaint of two practical, white fishermen as to their trouble, that they could not get gear because the canneries had very naturally decided not to employ as many as before. I am sorry the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not in his seat, but I think I see the minister without portfolio, the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiverin), and he will recall in Vancouver, before a delegation of the cannery men who interviewed him, that I gave this explanation of the situation on the Skeena river; that I invited contradiction if my statements were contrary
The Budget-Mr. Neill

to the facts in any way and that I received no contradiction. I will give the real reason why the cannery men prefer the Japs. The reason is two-fold and very natural too. One is that the Japs are much more convenient to deal with. The white men are unfortunately not amalgamated; the cannery men cannot deal with them in a body. They ought to be amalgamated. But the Japs are; the cannery man sends for the boss Jap, and in a few hours he can complete the whole arrangements for his season's work. He says to the boss Jap: "I want so many Japs for fishing licenses. I want so many to work in the canneries. I want so many to make a contract to fill the cans and pack them," and so on, and that is the end of his troubles for that year. The boss Jap attends to all the rest. If a Jap dies or disappears, the white employer never hears about the event. Another one is put at once in his place. This saves the cannery man a great deal of trouble, I quite admit. The other reason is that the Japs are probably Cheaper, in this way. The white man demands better accommodation. He will not live in a shack let alone permit his wife to live in one, as the Japs will. A Jap and his wife and eight or nine children will live in one small shack and be quite happy under sanitary conditions that a white man would not tolerate. I well recall the surprise on the faces of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) when they went into a cannery one day and saw Japanese women, with babies from three weeks to nine months old strapped on their backs, putting up the salmon in cans. We were used to this, but it was a revelation to them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I sent the babies home.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
People in the east say: It is a funny thing that virile white men cannot compete with the Japanese in British Columbia. That and similar reasons are why we cannot. We do not want to subject our women and children to living under such conditions of life and work. For that reason, it is naturally cheaper for the cannery men to employ Japs because their quarters are much cheaper in that regard.
The cannery men are primarily interested in getting Japs 'back to use gill nets. They are not at all interested in the herring branch of the industry. There are 1,179 Japs who got gill net licenses last year. They are all allocated to different canneries pro rata. There are something like sixty-five canneries, so that they would average from nineteen to twenty Japs to each cannery. They do

not always get that number, but that is an average and the department is proposing this year to impose a further restriction on these Japanese of only 15 per cent. Fifteen per cent out of nineteen or twenty comes to less than three, but we will call it three. That is the extent of the trouble and embarrassment that is proposed to be imposed upon these canneries-to replace this year three more Japs with three white people. The canning industry supports, it is said, 17,000 people in British Columbia. We ask to cut down these gill net workers by 180 this year, or only three to each cannery, and that is what all the trouble and fuss is about, all this propaganda and talk of ruin of the canning industry, because of employing three fewer Japs in a cannery on an average and three more white men. I have more data that I could give that would be illuminating, but I will not give it now because I think I can contend that the cannery men have not made out a good case for the increased use of the Japanese.
These cannery men, as I quite admit, have their own troubles. I believe they are oppressed by a case tax which, I think, is too heavy, and I would also like to see the sales tax taken off, not only for their benefit, but for the benefit of all the working people, because canned salmon is the poor man's food. I have, time and again, urged and I will again in the future urge that change on the government, particularly a reduction of the case tax which is very unjust to the cannery men. I would be delinquent in my duty as a representative even from the district, let alone from the province, if I did not do everything I could to advocate the interests of the canning industry and of these same cannery men about whom I have been talking. I realize they have an enormous investment. As regards their business and the employment they give, their industry is of the greatest importance. I do not minimize in the least the consideration they ought to get; I am prepared to support them in every legitimate manner, and I have done so as the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) knows. But there is such a thing as being fair to both sides, and the cannery men should recognize that they owe something to the people of British Columbia by trying to help to make this industry a white man's one in years to come.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has made out his case against the cannery men, but in the representations which some of us have received, the question is not so much

The Budget-Mr. Neill
of keeping the Japanese out of the province or out of one industry, as, having excluded them from one industry, what is to become of them? The representations which I have received are that the government, by interfering with the business in the hardships of which they naturally engage, are forcing these men to go into some other industries more congenial to white men, such as the growing of small fruits, and I have communications from various sources complaining that the government are driving them out of the fishing business; driving them off the high seas and forcing them into the more congenial atmosphere of the small-fruit business. The hon. member made a considerable study of the question and other hon. gentlemen would be interested to know his views on this point: the Japanese being in the province, where will legislation cease in directing their activities?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I should hardly like the
hon. member to leave the impression that I had made out any case against the cannery men; I am here simply to say that they have not made out their case so far as the restriction is concerned. As regards the other points to which the hon. member has alluded, I shall deal with them shortly. But I will say that I, too, have received suggestions that these men are being driven into the berrygrowing business, but I have traced the allegation to its source in one instance and I find that it does not come from the berry men themselves but from a paid lawyer of the Japanese. And that naturally vitiates to a great extent any weight it might have. It is all very well to contend that they should not be allowed to compete with the berry growers, but that objection should come from the berry growers themselves and not from the Japanese; otherwise it loses all its force. It is like the man who went to the council of a certain town and put up a strong plea to have the place made a horseless town. The town council were much impressed but the representation lost a good deal of its weight when it was discovered that this man was the garage owner in the town. The same principle applies in this case. Let us wait until the berry men complain and then I will pay more attention to the representations that are then made. I want to be sure, not that the man who is making those reresenta-tions is speaking on behalf of the berry men but that the berry men are actually complaining themselves; I want the berry men's
O.K. to the complaint.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Although the hon. member has not ascertained the facts himself, he must
know that if you take five hundred or a thousand Japanese from the fishing industry they must find work somewhere else. My question is, how does he propose to handle that phase of their activities?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I shall deal with that question later. As regards the herring business, that is in the hands of a totally different class of .people. I may observe here that they do not can herrings to any great extent out there; they dry-salt the fish in a very primitive way. The herring packers were told last year that they would have to employ twenty-five per cent of whites or Indians in their crews on the seine -boats on the east coast of Vancouver island. On the west coast for nearly ten years all the employees on herring seines have been white men and no disaster has occurred. I can recall the time the Japanese were taken off the salmon seines some years ago; they were removed one hundred per cent in a single season, and although disaster was prophesied nothing untoward happened. In the present case the trouble arises from the fact that the Japanese have been told that twenty-five per cent of their employees on the herring seines on the east coast of Vancouver island must be white men or Indians. There has been some propaganda in that connection but I shall not delay the House to discuss it. However, the Japanese sent in two petitions in that regard both of which I have studied with considerable care. The stuff that I got from some of the white men I threw into the wastepaper basket as being unworthy of consideration; they were talking nonsense. But the Japanese put up a reasonably worded plea and I gave it all the attention it deserved. They stressed two main contentions, the first of which was that only Japanese could, fish profitably in this particular spot on the east coast of the island. They stated that there was a place where the tide ran so strong that it called for the greatest skill in handling the boats. There was a frequent change in the tide, one current below another, and that it was impossible for anyone to man a boat there unless he had thorough experience as a fisherman. It was stated further that the bottom was rocky and required very skilful and experienced men. And so on. At this particular place which it is said is so exceedingly difficult to navigate, a spot called the Gap in the constituency of my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie), there is never any very great catch; some years they have taken no more than fifty tons per net in the whole season. So that it would not much matter if that place were eliminated. Now, I admit that in these particular waters, as in every
The Budget-Mr. Neill

industry, experienced men are required. But the point with which I take issue is the implication that white men or Indians cannot be taught to fish in this spot or anywhere else. The Indian has been all his life more or less on the water and there is no reason under the sun why he should not gain experience enough to handle boats here or anywhere else. Is there some peculiar fetish about that one particular spot in all the wide world that white men cannot learn to fish there? That is the Japanese argument and it falls to the ground the moment it is stated. The fact is, of course, that the Japanese employers do not want to get rid of their countrymen, and last year they complied with the law nominally; twenty-five per cent of their employees were white men. But they took these men on and never gave them any opportunity to get into the hang of handling the nets under these particular conditions. White men in a similar situation would have looked to the future and seen to it that the inexperienced fishermen should learn to handle the nets so that the following year they might be able to do the work properly. But the Japanese did not do that; they kept these white men on the pay roll in order nominally at least to comply with the law while their Japanese countrymen continued fishing. They were able therefore to say to the fishery officer, "We have tried the white men and they have proved a failure". And naturally the white men failed under those conditions; they were not given a chance to acquire the local experience. I want to quote a few sentences from a letter I received from a man who gave evidence before the Fisheries Commission over which my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) so ably presided,-and I remember that the hon. gentleman as chairman of the commission commented on the intelligent way in which this man had given his evidence. He says:
Enclosed please find clipping from a Vancouver paper.
The clipping reads:
The weight of evidence shows-
And there is no weight of evidence at all.
-that neither whites nor Indians can handle herring nets successfully on the rocky east coast of Vancouver island, it is stated.
This correspondent goes on to say:
I enclose clipping which is an outrage and entirely untrue, and no doubt you will agree when you read it. It practically says that a white man or Indian don't know or cannot catch herring by the purse seine method on the east coast of Vancouver island. Well, sir, for your information I would say that the white man taught the Jap how to catch herring there many years ago, and myself was one of those that they learned from by watching us. And also in regard to the new

law passed last June making it compulsory for the salteries and seine owners to use 25 per cent whites or Indians: it is a good law and will ultimately give back to the white fishermen and Indian that which they have been gradually edged out of for years. I have been identified with the fisheries over 35 years on this coast and am absolutely fed up with the way the white man has been edged out of his inheritance, namely, the fishing industry of British Columbia and compelled to go to the States to get a living on account of the Japanese. We want that law pertaining to herring fishing and salting left just as it is. Give the white fisherman a chance and he will soon show them whether he can catch the fish or not.
I have also a telegram which I should like to read. I wrote to a man, sending him a copy of the Japanese petition asking for his opinion. This is his answer:
B.C., 30-31 March, 1925.
A. W. Neill, M.P.
Sir, your letter just been read to me over the wire am on my way fishing will be gone two weeks can contradict all statements made by Japanese and supply proof we have fished salmon successfully in those very waters under the same conditions I will write full statement upon return.
This I think answers the contention that they cannot use whites or Indians; they can. The other contention has somewhat more weight: it is urged on behalf of the boss men or packers, not the individual fishers; it is said that they were the pioneers and it is unfair to freeze them out. That is an argument that appeals to any white man. I considered that carefully too, but it is untenable, in this regard: we are not seeking to drive out Japanese capital; we are not seeking to drive them out of the business at all. In fact, we are quite willing they should remain. It is true they cannot get individual herring net licenses in their own names, but they can do what a good many of them have already done -form a company with a few white men at the head and by mortgage or some other control continue in the business. All we ask is that they employ white men. That is not an unreasonable request. On the west coast they have employed for years all white men on these herring boats owned by Japanese, these boats taking their fish into Japanese plants. So there is no trouble in that respect.
Another contention they made was that they are best qualified to deal with this trade, that it is in a way peculiar to them because they understand the oriental market and handle the trade over there. I want to explain that. The market for these herrings is not in Japan at all,-if it is it is for a very small amount; the ultimate market is in China, principally in southern China, and these Japs ship the herrings over to Japan, I suppose, and tranship them to China. In reply to the implication that if we interfere with them too much we may lose this very important business, let

The Budget-Mr. Neill
me quote a telegram which I received the other day from a government official:
Student class in southern China prevent any dried salt herring of Japanese origin being marketed there, and correspondence and newspaper despatchs from Orient mention destruction of shipment suspected of Japanese origin.
When they find there any of this dry-salted herring coming in which they suspect of being handled by the Japanese they take it out and burn it. I have an extract from a letter written by a Chinese merchant to his agent in Vancouver, expressing the same idea. He practically says: For heaven's sake don't let it be known they are handled by Japanese. Let me quote one or two sentences:
In case you cannot secure space of direct steamer you should tranship the goods to us either through Hongkong or Shanghai. This commodity should not be shipped in a Japanese steamer as we do not like its name appeared in the bill of lading and other documents.
In order to remove suspicion, we wish you to mark the boxes according to the sample which we sent you on July 5, 1924. It should be also marked "origin of Canada" on the box. The seal of the government should be used if possible.
We believe that you will be pleased to help us from difficulty. We wish you to write a letter to the British Consul and ask him to remove the difficulty or suspicion *of your product as Japanese goods. The Chinese officials and the chamber of commerce should be made to understand that the fish is a Canadian product not Japanese product.
It is evident that the ultimate market for this commodity is in China. The Chinese merchants are willing to buy it from white men, and they are very much afraid that any shipment should be suspected of being of Japanese origin. So I do not think we need put much weight on the Japanese contention that the market may be lost if they do not get the privileges they are asking for.
Now I come to the argument of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), the argument advanced by the Japanese, that these men who will be taken out of the fishing industry will go into the berry industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I do not wish it to appear on record that the Japanese have advanced this argument to me. The argument has been advanced by people interested in the fruit and other industries. They say that already the Japanese who are being driven out of the fishing industry are crowding into these other industries. What solution does the hon. member suggest for this trouble?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I entirely disclaim any suggestion of making a personal reference to the hon. member. My mind was so full of the correspondence I have received that I was applying it to these correspondents and not
in any way reflecting on the hon. gentleman himself. I have no doubt that he has letters of the character he indicates. Now I want to deal with that argument. I have heard it stated that some of the Japanese have gone north to Siberia to engage in fishing there. I do not know what weight may be attached to the statement, but I think practically little. I am willing to admit that most of these Japanese must find other occupations. But there are 60,000 orientals in British Columbia, and taking 200 out of the salmon industry each year is not going to create any particular hardship when they are spread over the 60,000 engaged in other industries. What is of far -more importance is the constant importation of orientals. The restrictions do not run quite so high in number as he thinks, but what is the use of restricting a couple of hundred from the salmon industry if the Japanese are coming in by their thousands every year? There is where the leakage is, and that is where we want to stop it. But I want to deal with that point still further, and to draw particular attention to the first two paragraphs of a resolution passed by the British Columbia legislature. The resolution itself is a long one and I will ask permission of the House to place it on Hansard. I think it may be fairly stated that when the legislature of any province passes a resolution lit pretty well represents the provincial point of view on the subject matter dealt with. This is the most drastic anti-oriental resolution that I ever saw the British Columbia legislature pass, and I have seen them pass a good many in years gone by.
Therefore be it Resolved. That this House go on record as being utterly opposed to the further influx of Orientals into this province, and further, that this House places itself on record as being in favour of the enactment of such amendment to the "Immigration Act of Canada," as is necessary to completely prohibit Asiatic immigration into Canada.
Be it further Resolved, That this House is also of the opinion that the field of industrial and commercial activities of all Orientals now in Canada, particularly British Columbia, should be restricted by legislation.
And be it further Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Honour the Lieutenant-Governor, praying that he cause a copy of this Resolution to be transmitted to the Hon. the Secretary of State or other proper official at Ottawa, for presentation to His Excellency the Governor General in Council.
Be it further Resolved, That the government of the Dominion of Canada be respectfully requested to grant adherence on the part of Canada to no treaty or binding international obligation in any form whatsoever having the effect of limiting the authority or power of Provincial Legislatures in respect of the regulation of social and industrial activities within the provinces; and, further that the government of the Dominion of Canada be respectfully requested to forthwith take the action necessary to bring about the denunciation of any and all treaties in so far as the terms and provisions of the same have the effect of
The Budget-Mr. Neill

depriving the Dominion of Canada of the power of regulation, control and prohibition of Asiatic immigration?
You see, they recognize the continuance of this restrictive policy in all lines of business. This resolution was passed by the British Columbia legislature on December 17 last, and I want to point out the peculiar conditions of the vote. If you look at the records of the British Columbia House, you will find that something hatppened which I never heard of before in any legislature in the world. There was a vote forced-we know how that is done-and the vote as it appeared was 43 yeas; against, nil. A number of people all of the same mind, 43 of them, forced a vote in order to have it recorded that they were there and voted in that way. The journals of the House go on record that there were three members absent, and they named those men, bringing the -membership up to 46; there was one member deceased, and there was the Speaker in the -chair, these accounting -for the complete membership of 48. It shows the determination of those men to get themselves on record when they compelled a vote on a matter in regard to which there was no opposition. I think you will find the politician in British Columbia always has his ear to the ground and knows what his constituents at home think about the matter. I also draw attention to the fact that those -members were in (favour of further restrictions at that time. Still it may be held that I have not completely answered the objection of the hon. member for Vancouver South in regard to the berry growers. Perhaps he -will accept the evidence of the berry farmers themselves. On February 17 and 18, 1925, the United Farmers of British Columbia met at Revelstoke and passed -a lon-g resolution, which I want to place on Hansard:
Whereas the Oriental population in B. C. is estimated at 60,000 owning or leasing 26,000 acres of land, and if allowed to continue uncontrolled will surely soon force the remaining white vegetable growers off the land, and in so doing strike at the very base of the structure of the white population, and
Whereas the refusal of the Orientals, excepting the majority of the Japanese, who are good co-operators, although supplanting white people on the land, to join the co-operative marketing organizations on the success of which the best hopes of the vast majority of the white fruit and vegetable growers are centred, nullifies the efforts of these organizations, and
Whereas in fishing, lumbering and retailing and many other lines of business they are, by industry and pricecutting, ousting white competitors living at Canadian standards, and
Whereas it is estimated that Orientals export to their home countries through banks and post offices $16,000.000 annually, thus robbing Canadian trade, and
Whereas a homogeneous and not a dual population is in the best interests of Canada, both for strength of the nation in war and its institutions in peace.

Therefore, be it resolved by the delegates of the United Farmers of B. C. in convention at Revelstoke, February 17 and 18, 1925, that they support the resolution on exclusion of Orientals sent to Ottawa by the B. C. government, and earnestly urge the prohibiting of the owning or leasing of land in Canada by Orientals, and the passing of such further legislation as will tend to eliminate Orientals from competitive business in Canada.
I would direct the attention of hon. members to the concluding paragraph. Far from wanting this restriction on Japs cut out, they want it extended, and they say, "Eliminate orientals from competitive business." Further, they want the same principle extended to the holding of agricultural land in Canada. I think that goes far enough. Vv hat they want is the same restriction as was passed in California, a law prohibiting orientals from owning or leasing -land for agricultural purposes. That of course is a provincial -matter, and I only quote -it to show that the United Farmers of British Columbia are not unwilling to restrict oriental participation in the fish industry; only they wa-nt the restriction applied to them further.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
made any inquiry as to the right oi a province to pass such legislation, in view of the existence of the Japanese treaty?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
That, Mr. Speaker, is somewhat beside the subject, and I am taking up a good deal of time, but I suppose I am in order to answer. Yes, I have made investigations in that regard, and I believe it would be entirely intra vires of -the province to pass such legislation. Here is the Japanese treaty referred to; section 4 says:
They-
That is, nationals of either race.
-shall be permitted to own or hire and occupy houses, manufactories. . . . and to lease land for residential, commercial, industrial and other lawful purposes, in the same manner as native subjects.
It has been held by legal luminaries that that extends to the buying or leasing of land for any purpose of business, factories and so on. The next section is the one which I think applies to agricultural land. It says:
They shall, on condition of reciprocity, be at full liberty to acquire and possess every description of property.
And so on. I would call attention to the words "on condition of reciprocity." That is to say, "You can do what we do." Now, the Japanese law does not allow a white man to lease or own land for agricultural purposes in Japan, though he may do so for industrial purposes. So that it is thoroughly competent for us, since they do not allow us to do it,

The Budget-Mr. Neill
to prevent their doing it in British Columbia.
I took this point up with one of the best legal advisers of the crown here, and he expressed the opinion that the point was well taken. He said it could not be finally decided, however, until appeal was taken to the Privy Council and he suggested I should try to get some local interest in British Columbia stirred up in the matter. I am glad to say that I have interested one of the local members of the riding I represent and he has promised to bring the matter up in the British Columbia legislature at the next sitting. I have taken too long, Mr. Speaker, in dealing with this matter, but I wanted to show that these restrictions, which were applied on the recommendation of an impartial commission, were conceived in wisdom and have been carried out with fairness and moderation and without doing injury to any industry.
I said earlier in my remarks that I wanted to deal with the record of the government in this regard, and I was pointing out what the government had done in fulfilment of the resolution and the pledges they gave. I said they had passed the Chinese Immigration Act, which is all to the good and most successful. I said they had passed the restrictions to which I have referred, and which are good so far as they have gone. The third thing they have done is to reduce the quota. Now, there is a clause in the gentleman's agreement-I have it here, but I shall not bother reading it-that says that not more than 400-at that time-agricultural labourers or domestic or personal servants shall be allowed by the Japanese government to come into Canada per annum. The quota, it will be noted, applied to these two classes only. Last year the government of the day cut that number down to 150, but unfortunately the door is still wide open for some classes other than these two, such as women and children, and families, to come in practically without any limitation. I shall not waste the time of the House in debating this subject. It is almost an established fact that in that regard the gentleman's agreement is now at any rate a failure.
