And I may say that while I was praising the officials a moment ago for the manner in which they handled the Chinese Immigration Act, I cannot say the same as regards the Japanese. They seem ito look upon Japanese immigration, coming, as it does, under the gentleman's agreement, as something that does not interest them. I do not know that they even have a copy of the gentleman's agreement, and they do not seem to understand its vague provisions very clearly. At any rate they do not seem to pay the 113
regard to its enforcement that they have given to the restrictions under the Chinese Immigration Act. Last year the quota was put at 150. The returns I got in the House the other day show that 146 came in, but that is not the whole story. If I took the time I could show that on the face of it at least 37 of the 146 came in illegally. But what is the use of arguing about that when 262 women came in, and one or two more hundreds in the way of families? Boys of seventeen, as many as you like, can come in-and you cannot tell whether a Jap boy is seventeen or twenty-one-under the guise of being members of families. A Japanese boy can say: "lama member of the family of so and so that was here twenty years ago," and he has to be admitted. So I shall not take the time to deal with that phase of the subject; there is no doubt the condition is far from satisfactory.
Now, these are the three things that the government have done. They have all been good, and they have constituted a wide departure from the record of previous governments in this regard. But I hope the government wiil not think me ungracious when I say that while these provisions are good, they are not enough. The people of British Columbia have become aroused. This propaganda has attracted attention and ha's created a sort of reaction. The people are beginning to sit up and take notice; they are saying they want these things looked into; they demand action. I have numerous telegrams and letters, but I shall refer to but two of them. Here is one from The Native Sons:
We look for definite action on Japanese immigration at the present session.
That is the key-note of their demand- action; action this session. Here is another one from 607 Canadian women meeting in Vancouver-I am glad to see the women of Canada interested in this subject. They say, "Enthusiastically endorse stand," and they demand that during the present session action be taken. That is the key-note of them all. They refer back to the resolution of 1922 and to the assurance given us on July 11 of last year by the Prime Minister, and they ask that action be taken.
Now, as regards a method, I will suggest one simple method for the consideration of the government. It would be quite easy. Any Japanese coming to Canada has to have a passport signed by a Japanese official in Japan; that, I believe, is the law to-day. All that is needed, therefore, is a small addition, one more regulation by agreement with the Japanese government, to the effect that when

The Budget-Mr. Neill

a Japanese arrives in British Columbia he must produce a passport not only signed by the Japanese official in Japan but also vised by the Canadian consul there as well, with the understanding-the latent understanding, if you like-that the Canadian official is never to put his vise on it. There is the thing in a nutshell. It would have the advantage of not requiring legislation. It would save the face of the Japanese; there is precedent for it; it could not be called offensive; they could agree to it, you might say, in an informal manner, and there would be no need for the strong terms employed by the United States which gave so much offence to the Japanese. If something of that kind were passed I believe it would absolutely meet the case. One addition, perhaps, that I would suggest to it would be this: If possible some system of registration should be adopted such as we had when the Chinese Immigration Act came into effect. When the Chinese registration was being carried out it was discovered that 25 per cent more Chinamen were in Canada than there should have been according to the records. I do not say we should do that with regard to the Japanese with any idea of making trouble for those who are now in Canada; I would leave them at liberty, but I would use it to prevent smuggling, to which there would be great temptation following the making of any such provision as I have suggested.
Now is the time, as never before, for action, and I believe I am speaking in the interest of Japan as well as of Canada when I say so. It is not wise to wait until there is a flaring up of public opinion, like there was in the United States, and then to pass, in a moment perhaps, some drastic measure of exclusion which the Japanese would consider of an insulting character. It should be explained to them quietly and determinedly that if they will not agree to some measure of effective restriction of this character, then they must expect that sooner or later we will follow in the footsteps of the United States. Other nations are tightening up in the matter of oriental immigration. I have been in communication with other dominions and other countries and I find that increasingly the case. In Africa, where the conditions are much worse than here, long-years ago the situation got so bad that they absolutely excluded any oriental immigration. But they have come to the stage now where they have a system of what they call voluntary repatriation. The Asiatic problem there is not Japanese, but has to do with the natives of India. They have a system by which in some provinces particularly those in which IMr. Neill.]
the orientals are so numerous that they outnumber the white people, they say to any Indians who want to go home to India: "We will pay your fare from the centre of Africa, if need be, to the point of embarkation. We will pay your steamship fare to India. We will pay jrnur railway fare to even the most remote part of India when you get there, and when you have arrived at your native village we will give you 850 in cash, and our blessing." That has been in force some years. The official who wrote me that remarked dryly that they had almost arrived at the limit of the success of that plan. They had repatriated as many as would go voluntarily, and there was talk of making it compulsory in the future. There is the situation we are coming to if we do not take time by the forelock.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is an election in the air; I can smell signs of it. This is the period in the life of this parliament, as in all parliaments, when it becomes good politics for an independent party or an independent member to attack the government. The time is arriving when not much more can be expected from the government in the way of needed legislation or government grants-and it is always popular to attack a government anyway. If a member is independent and supports the government, of course he is called a truckler, if he opposes it he is called a patriot, and they say that is a sign of his sincerity. Sometimes it is; sometimes it is only a sign of his moral weakness. I recall the case of a magistrate who told me that he had a case before him in which his brother was concerned, and he said that he had given the decision against his brother, although he thought he was in the right, because he did not want to be accused of favouring a blood relation. He thought by that he showed his independence and his courage. I thought he showed his cowardice and moral weakness. It was just as bad to be afraid of popular opinion as to be influenced by his domestic relation. I could follow in the footsteps, perhaps, of the Progressive party when they moved an amendment the other day expressing their opinion of the government. I have it here, and it is a very drastic expression indeed. Of course it was out of order, but if I believed that the government of this day were as bad as this represents them to be, I think I would long ere this have been actively engaged in some line of action calculated to overthrow them. I could very easily draw up an amendment with the knowledge that you will rule it out of order, Mr. Speaker, and that it would not unduly embarrass the

The Budget-Mr. Duff
government. I could outline in that amendment a number of policies that would be very popular in my district, and could add a fiery denunciation of the government for not carrying them out. In that way I might obtain some cheap publicity for the moment among a few unthinking people. But the bulk of my constituents are not unthinking people, they are hard-headed, clear-thinking people, and I do not think they would fall for that sort of thing. They are not interested in long-drawn-out, fine-spun debates of theories and academic questions. They are not easily caught by claptrap oratory.

Now, instead of condemning the government for not acting as quickly as I and other members from British Columbia would like them to have acted in the matter of oriental exclusion, I am going to take a chance on the government and say that I believe they and more particularly the Prime Minister, are
sincere in this matter. I believe that he will at this session carry out the mandate given by the resolution of 1922, emphasized by the assurances he gave us in the debate of last July. Whilst I agree with what he said about the fishery situation in British Columbia, I find myself not in entire agreement with his remarks last night in regard to what should be done in the defence of our shores, both on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. However, I am sure that the hon. gentleman was sincere in his opinions with regard to the defence of the sea coasts of this country, and consequently I am not going to raise any objection at this late hour to what he said in that connection.
With regard to the fishery situation in British Columbia-and the hon. member for Comox-Albemi deserves the congratulations of this House for the able manner in which he presented his opinions-I, as chairman of the commission which went out to British Columbia some two or three years ago and made some recommendations to the government, should like to say a few words with regard to the other gentlemen who were on that commission. Being chairman, my whole duty was to sit in the chair and see that the other commissioner's kept order; it was these other gentlemen who did the work, Mr. Speaker, and I have very much pleasure even at this late date in saying that the commission, comprised of five other members besides the chairman, did good work for the fisheries of British Columbia, and I might add that it cost only about half as much as any other
The Budget-Mr. Duff

commission which investigated fishery conditions in that province.
Now may I deal for a few minutes with the budget and with matters which have been taken up during the debate. The only matter with which I intend to deal is in regard to what the government has endeavoured to do for the province of Nova Scotia, and the announcement which the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) made in that regard in presenting his budget. In this budget, Sir, the government in a very practical way has endeavoured to show the people of Nova Scotia that it is in sympathy with them, and the legislation which was introduced by the government with regard to the coal industry of this country,-and of course this applies to the coal industry in other provinces of this Dominion as well as Nova Scotia-certainly deserves from this parliament and the people of this country the highest commendations they can give. It will be remembered, Sir, that not only this year, but last year, the government tried to do something for the province of Nova Scotia. Last year this House voted the sum of S200,000 towards reducing the freight rates on coal, so that Nova Scotia coal could be taken to the 5 p.m. markets of upper Quebec and Ontario. The people of Nova Scotia Were able to take advantage of that grant made by the government to the extent that Nova Scotia coal was able to be carried one hundred miles farther west than it had been carried in previous years. The government this year have gone one step further, and have introduced a resolution with regard to using slack coal for coking purposes. 1 do not know whether I am in order in dealing with this question, but I wish to say in [DOT]passing that the people of Nova Scotia, and In fact the people of all provinces where coal 3s mined, should certainly express thanks to the government and this parliament for introducing and passing that legislation. In addition to that, when the tariff was brought down, the government increased the duty on slack coal from fourteen to fifty cents a ton. Whilst I am a great believer in low tariff-and if it were possible I would like to see no tariff in this country-yet as long as we have a tariff I see no objection to raising the duty on slack coal and putting it on a level with the duty on the other coal. I think the government has in a practical way shown the people of Nova Scotia and the people of Cape Breton, where most of the coal is mined, that they believe in dealing with these questions in a practical manner, and they are not carried away by what they read in the newspapers 
or what they hear, but they sit down, I might say, in conference with the members from the Maritime provinces, who in the newspapers for the last several months have been criticized for not going out every day and giving interviews and telling what they have done. It is only fair to say that the Maritime province members and especially the members from Nova Scotia have for the last two or three years endeavoured to get the government to do something in regard to this coal question in Nova Scotia, and I think the government, with the legislation which they have introduced and are now introducing, have shown in a practical manner that their sympathies are with the coal miners of Nova Scotia as well as the coal miners of other provinces of the Dominion.
We listened last evening to a speech made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). I fail to see, Mr. Speaker, what the remarks of that hon. member had to do with the budget; but in view of the fact that there were perhaps sentimental reasons why you did not want to call this hon. member to order and let her proceed, I trust you will, treat me with the same courtesy and consideration this afternoon, as I think it is only fair that the other side of this question should be given, not only to this House but to the country. There is no question, that during the last few weeks there has been a great deal said pro and con regarding the coal situation in Nova Scotia, and the situation in mining areas of that district. I was very much struck with a remark made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey last evening. You will perhaps remember, sir, that in the course of her address, when speaking of conditions in Cape Breton and the situation of the miners there, she mentioned the fact that the miners were a proud people and did not wish to aocept charity or help from anybody. That is quite true. It is a matter of history that the Scotch are a proud race. But it must not be forgotten that not only are the miners of Cape Breton a proud race but the people of Nova Scotia are a proud race. Whilst we are a hospitable people and welcome anybody within our gates, yet as I said a moment ago we are a proud people, and we resent undue interference from outsiders. I have no desire whatever to criticize the hon. member, in view of the fact that she is alone in one regard in this House-

The hon. member for Southeast Grey gave some individual cases and told us what she had seen in the Cape Breton area. It is quite true a strike has been in progress there for some time, but even if a strike were not in progress there would necessarily be some destitution and some poverty in an area of that size. Now after hearing her remarks and reading what she said,

What did she say? Now who is he, pray? She said also, in denouncing the provincial government and in denouncing the parliamentarians, that the Labour party had no representative in parliament. Evidently, this hon. member did not get in the right company or was not told the correct story in the right company, because the mayor of Glace Bay is a member of parliament in the province of Nova Scotia and is known as a Labour member of parliament. There are also two other Labour members from the county of Cape Breton in the parliament of Nova Scotia and, if I am not mistaken, one from the county of Cumberland. This lady was imet by the mayor of Glace Bay, and evidently from what she tells us, the mayor of Glace Bay, who is the Labour member from that city, put her on the track to find out where all this destitution and poverty existed. What does she find out? She finds but that people are hungry after a three weeks' strike. It is quite natural that some people would be hungry after a three weeks' strike, but she did not go into the particulars and find out how many people in that district were not hungry after a three weeks' strike. She did not find out that the heads of twenty families, who are getting relief from the relief committee in the town of Glace Bay to-day, had $5,000 each in tin-bank. She did not find out this, for instance.

She told of homes where there were only two bedrooms, a kitchen and a sitting room. How many members in this House-and I hope I am not going to say anything now that will offend anyone-and how many of their grandfathers or forefathers were raised in any bigger houses than houses with two bedrooms, a kitchen and a sitting room? How many fishermen in British Columbia or Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick have homes with more than two bedrooms on the second floor and, perhaps, an attic for five or six children? How many people have only two bedrooms, a sitting room and a kitchen? It is silly for anyone to come into this House and talk about conditions like these. These conditions prevail everywhere. These people do not live in palaces; but if they had been a little more economical, maybe they would have been able to add an L to their kitchen or another bedroom over the L. The hon. member for Southeast Grey told us about an awfful house on the bluff at Glace Bay where she said a man and his family were living under terrible conditions. She said that there w'as practically no roof on this house; that it was leaking, but that this man had to pay $20 a month for it. I do not wish to say anything with regard to the statement by the hon. member for Southeast Grey, especially for a certain reason; but she is certainly gullible and she must think we are gullible when she says in this House that any miner or fisherman or lumberman or workingman in Nova Scotia can afford to pay $20 a month for the best house that can be obtained. Instead of paying $20 a month, the most these miners pay is about $2 a week. Twenty dollars a month is $240 a year. Yet the mayor of Glace Bay, who is a Labour member for Cape Breton, assisted by his truant officer-and I do not know the particular reason why the mayor of Glace Bay put the hon. member in charge of a truant officer-told her that this poor fellow had to pay $20 a month for his house.
What other awful things did she tell us? She told us about visiting one family where there was tuberculosis; the mother was suffering from this dread disease, and the hon. member deplored the fact that a woman with tuberculosis should be allowed to sleep in the same room with the rest of her family. Now. I would suggest that before the hon. member undertakes to give us the pleasure of her presence in Nova Scotia she should
at least take the trouble to study to some extent the legislation of that province so far as it relates to the matters she investigates. There is no reason whatever why anyone with tuberculosis in an advanced stage should remain at home either in Glace Bay or anywhere else in the province. We have a splendid institution at Kentville and if this doctor to whom the hon. member referred, or the great friend of hers, the mayor of Glace Bay, or the truant officer, had done their duty by themselves and by this poor woman they would have had her sent to the sanitarium instead of having her remain at home with her children.
The hon. member also talked about the terrible condition of the streets, about the sewerage and about other things of that nature. She said1 there was no electric light in the town; whilst there were lights and a few sidewalks in the centre of the town there was no light on the outskirts. She also told us that there was a lot of mud in the place. Well, we are told that there are good roads in Ontario; but going through the province the other day I spent some ten hours gazing out of the car window, and as my eyes turned from one side of the landscape to the other, this being the first time I had passed through that part of the country, I beheld very muddy roads indeed. And are there not muddy roads in Quebec and in every other province in the Dominion just as there are in Nova Scotia? Surely it is nothing out of the way to see muddy roads in the outskirts of any town especially at this time of year. Indeed, we have a clause in the Road Act in Nova Scotia prohibiting the running of automobiles at this time of year, the reason being I suppose that owing to weather conditions the roads are too muddy. Yet the hon. member tried to impress upon the House the other evening the awful condition in which she found the roads in that Nova Scotian town.

Yet my hon. friend who interrupts me suggests that the mayor of that town did his full duty when he called a session of the council and voted $5,000 for the relief of four or five thousand suffering people-a dollar apiece.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: In view of the hon. gentleman's strictures on the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) in this regard, I would ask him whether he does not think that the company, as the landlord of these miner tenants, also has some responsibility for the sanitary conditions in the town?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
They are responsible for the
sanitary conditions in the tenements which they own, but they have no right to install any system of sewerage in the town, to provide electric lights, or to do anything of that kind. Those things are under the control of the town and there is no reason why the company should look after them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Does the hon.
member know that throughout the years the company has largely dominated the municipal councils?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I regret that my hon. friend
has been so gullible; certainly he does not know anything about the conditions that obtain down there. The hon. gentleman gets up on the floor of the House whenever he has an opportunity to say something about Nova Scotia, and it seems to me that before he does that he might give the conditions of the province some study. Why should any hon. member go to a truant officer in the town, as the hon. member for Southeast Grey did on this occasion, instead of consulting responsible citizens with a view to ascertaining the facts as they are? Let me say that the company has never dominated civic conditions in any districts in which it operates. But there is a Labour mayor and there is a Labour council in Glace Bay as there are in New WTaterford and in all the other places where the labourers predominate, and the company certainly does not control affairs there. Now, I admit that the company has its faults and I shall refer to that aspect of the question later on; I am not here to take sides.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: May I ask a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I want to get through at six
o'clock.

The Budget-Mr. Duff

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman' has
taken exception to the report made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail). I wonder if he would be prepared to make at Glace Bay the speech which he is now making in this House?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, anybody who
knows me knows that I would make a speech anywhere. To use the picturesque language of the hon. member for Southeast Grey last night, I would not care a damn where it was.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I never said that last
night.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, she used similar
language.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: , I will withdraw the remark, Mr. Speaker; it is not parliamentary.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
It was not parliamentary,
but it was "snappy," to use the word of the hon. member for Southeast Grey. Now, Sir,
I do not ask the Labour group in this House to take my word for conditions in Cape Breton. Let me read something which has been said by	a very prominent lady in
Toronto. She has close associations with the mining district and goes down there every year to spend the summer. Here is what she says:
Aroused by the letter appearing in Saturday's Globe from Miss Agnes Macphail, M.P., relative to conditions in the mining areas of Nova Scotia, Mrs. Florence Fraser, Tyndall Avenue, a resident of Sydney for a number of years, who spends each summer with relatives in Nova Scotia, declared yesterday that she could "show Miss Macphail conditions much different from those described in her story." Mrs. Fraser insisted that the reading public was obtaining highly colored stories, favorable to the miners.
"From what I read, Miss Macphail is not thoroughly conversant with the conditions under which miners are living in Nova Scotia," said Mrs. Fraser. "There are houses built by the company, containing seven rooms, with hot and cold water, electric lights, and a garago with every second one. These are not described to the people of Toronto, nor is it told to them that the rental is from $5 to $7 a month. Neither are they told that numbers of miners own their own automobiles.
"There is another matter," continued Mrs. Fraser. "The miners are not forced to deal in the company's stores. There is a fine co-operative store there, as well as other retail stores. There is no difference in prices as between the company's and the retail stores. If anything, they are lower in the company stores."
Mrs. Fraser said the shacks referred to by Miss Macphail were never intended for families. They were built, she said, for transient labor from Newfoundland.
So I think Mrs. Fraser, who, I presume, is a responsible citizen of Toronto-she does not
hesitate to give her name-should be listened to by the people of this country just as much as should the hon. member for Southeast Grey, who in my opinion came back with a prejudiced story because she was guided around Glace Bay by the Labour mayor and the truant officer.
Now, Sir, in her peroration the hon. member was not satisfied with discussing conditions in Glace Bay, she must have a crack at the provincial government. She said that that government was not doing its duty in this matter and was, to use her own choice language, afraid of Besco. I cannot see why anybody who wants the votes of the people of Nova Scotia should be afraid of Besco.
I cannot see why the government of Nova Scotia, whether Liberal or Tory, should not stand in with the miners in this district in preference to standing in with the company, and for this reason:	The situation in Cape
Breton not only affects the immediate district, it affects the whole province, and if the hon. premier, Mr. Armstrong, does not do what is right and proper in trjdng to settle the strike, and use his best efforts in the premises to improve conditions in Cape Breton, not only the people there but the people in every other constituency will certainly have something to say to him when he appeals to the province in June. So I would say that Hon. Mr. Armstrong and his government and the legislature certainly have more interest in this matter than has either the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) or the hon. member for Southeast Grey. Premier Armstrong lives in Nova Scotia, he has everything at stake; and when the hon. member for Southeast Grey states that he and his government are not doing their duty, it seems to me that it requires a good deal of assurance on her part.
But, Sir, it has been contended that this government and the provincial government should come to the relief of the distressed people in the mining districts of Nova Scotia. Let us see whether they should take action. I understand that legislation with regard to looking after the poor is different in some of the other provinces to what it is in Nova Scotia. In our province, where we have as good legislation, and perhaps in some cases more advanced legislation than, in some of the other provinces, there is a statute dealing specifically with poor relief. Chapter 50 of the revised statutes of Nova Scotia distinctly sets out that poor relief must be paid through the organization created either by the city council, the town council or the .municipal council for the locality; the .province has
The Budget-Mr. Duff

absolutely nothing to do -with it. Each city, town or 'municipality must provide its own relief, and the act sets forth how this should be done. At the sitting of the town or city council every year a poor committee is appointed from the members. They have full power to deal with any and all oases of distress which come to their knowledge, and have power to assess the municipality to cover the cost. As I said a moment ago, the British Empire Steel Corporation are assessed about seventy per cent of the total assessment in the mining districts in which they have their mines. Now, if this gentleman, the mayor of Glace Bay, was so anxious to alleviate this horrible suffering, as detailed and retailed by the memlber for Southeast Grey, all he had to do was to call a special meeting of the city council, pass a vote for the money required from time to time, put that money in the hands of the poor committee of the .municipality, and see that it was expended. Because, as you will observe, Mr. Speaker, after all, this horrible Besco would pay about seventy per cent of the cost, and about two-thirds of the remaining thirty per cent would be paid by the citizens of Glace Bay, the professional and commercial men and others who are not miners and do not want relief, and the miners themselves iwould pay only ten per cent of the total amount required. And yet the friend of the hon. member for Southeast Grey sits down and does nothing except vote j$5,000. A wonderful man he is to relieve t'he situation in the city of Glace Bay! All he has to do if he thinks this combination, this B-e-s-c-o, is such a horrible thing, is to go out and make it pay seventy cents of every dollar he wants for the poor and hungry in Glace Bay and the surrounding district. If that is the fact, then until that is done why should the provincial government interfere, or why should my good friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) get up every once in a while in the House and ask the government as to the situation	in regard	to	the coal	strike	inNova Scotia? I am sure my hon. friend, who is	possessed	of	a great	deal	of
this world's goods, has done his full duty by the poor and suffering of his province. While I have not seen his name in either the Halifax or the Ottawa papers indicating that a large subscription had been made either by himself or the bank which has done business with these miners in Nova Scotia and of which he is a director, I am sure the hon. junior member for Halifax has done his full duty. And if he has done his full duty, there 
may be an excuse for his asking the government why they do not d:o something. The hon. member is evidently very much interested in the strikers and their dependents in Cape Breton. He is perhaps the best known shipping man in the Maritime provinces, and he has always had a fine business. I remember -and I am not very old-a longshoremen's strike in the city of Halifax. As hon. gentlemen know, longshoremen are hired to load and unload steamers and vessels and handle freight on the wharves. On the occasion of this strike, of course the loading and the unloading of the cargoes of vessels which came to the wharf of the hon. junior member for Halifax were affected. While my memory, perhaps, has become a little defective, I can remember that the hon. junior member for Halifax showed no great desire at that time either to settle the strike or to look after the wives and children of the men out on strike. Yet he gets up in has place now and day after day asks the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald)-I presume because he is the cabinet minister from Nova Scotia-what is being done with regard to these poor women and children in Cape Breton.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if the positions in connection with these two strikes are at all comparable?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: It is only a matter of degree.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
It is only a matter of degree. If fifty women and children were affected by the longshoremen's strike in Halifax and 20,000 are affected by the strike in Cape Breton, what is the difference so far as the position I have stated is concerned?
Now, what I say is this: The hon. member for Southeast Grey was good enough to say that the mayor of Glace Bay and the council there had voted the sum of $5,000; and I also noticed in the press this morning that this gentleman, who was a member of the local legislature, had hied himself to Halifax and asked for a special act 'to vote $5,000 for teachers' salaries,-you will remember that the hon. member for Southeast Grey told us last night that there was danger of the schools being closed because there was no money to pay salaries. Again I say she is not acquainted with Nova Scotia legislation. Anybody who knows anything about Nova Scotia legislation -and a school teacher, above all, should study legislation with regard to schools in

The Budget-Mr. Duff
other provinces as well as her own-should know that the school legislation in Nova Scotia provides that certain moneys shall be voted each year for the upkeep of the schools. For instance, in the town of Glace Bay some [DOT] time in February the council meets; they go over their requirements, and when they come to the question of schools they call in the school board, which is a separate organization from the city council, and they ask the school board how much money they require for the year. The school board tell them what money they require and the council put that amount in the estimates. I simply wish to make this point to show that somebody- now, I almost made a break that time-that somebody unquestionably fooled the member for Southeast Grey, because this money which was voted in February for the upkeep of schools provides for the upkeep of the schools, the payment of teachers' salaries, fuel, janitor and everything else, from the beginning of the school year in September until the next June. And she says this because the truant officer, in whose charge she was, or the mayor of Glace Bay, told her that there was no money to pay the school teachers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Did my hon. friend notice
a report in the press this morning that the council of Glace Bay had just voted another $5,000 with which to pay school teachers this month?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
No I did not, but I am glad
to hear it. Instead of voting another $5,000 they should vote $50,000 if necessary, because this poor Besco, this terrible organization, have to pay seventy per cent of it, and I shall be glad to see them pay it rather than that the women and children of Glace Bay should suffer. They ought to pay it because they are as much to blame for this strike, perhaps, as the miners are. I have no sympathy with Besco. All I want to do is to protect the good name of Nova Scotia and to see that no outsiders come in to interfere with us. Until such times as the town of Glace Bay does its duty by these women and children; until such time as the municipality does its duty by them; until such time as the province comes to their relief, it is not for anyone to get up on the floor of this House and ask for money or subscriptions from anybody.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
How can my hon. friend
protect the good name of Nova Scotia by casting aspersions on one of its chief citizens?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Who is that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: The mayor of Glace Bay.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I did not know that he was
one of its chief citizens. Anyone who will deliberately, for his own political purposes, allow women and children to starve, is no good citizen of this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
May I ask what
about the vice-president of Besco, who said that the people could not stand the gaff; that they had to come to the company?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I want to say that if I was
on the directorate of Besco I would have kicked Mr. MoLurg out of Cape Breton the minute he said that. He had no right to say it, and we will never have proper conditions until men like McLurg are kicked out of the company. But I say that is no reason why the hon. member for Southeast Grey should have made the reference she did last night to the three directors of the company who are members of the Senate and good citizens of this country. Let them clean up the mess; let them send McLurg about his business. He is not fit to have charge of anybody; I would not have him in charge of a henyard, let alone 12,000 miners in the county of Cape Breton. I have no sympathy with McLurg, not half as much, perhaps, as the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg has. Let him get out; let them put him out; the quicker the shareholders of the British Empire Steel Corporation get together and reorganize, the quicker we shall have industrial peace in Nova Scotia. All I am trying to do is to show that there is no necessity for all this political propaganda. It is not necessary for the hon. junior member for Halifax to come here and blow off every day about conditions in Cape Breton when there are fifteen other members from Nova Scotia in this House who are just as good men as he is and who have the interests of Nova Scotia and Cape Breton at heart. We are looking after this situation, and I for one will noit stand for it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: May I suggest that in this House we are all Canadians. Might I ask-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
May I ask if as a
Canadian I have not the right to protect the interests of other Canadians?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Is the hon. member rising
to a point of order?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
No, it is just a stray remark.
The Budget-Mr. Duff

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I am asking a
question, if I may, of the thon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
The hon. member may
ask it with the permission of the hon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
There is no question about
it, Mr. Speaker, that this is a free country and the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg has the right to get up, if he wants to, and talk about conditions in Ottawa or Prescott or L'Orignal or any place back in the woods. He can talk about anything he wants to. But the member for Prescott, (Mr. Binette), who represents in this House the people of that district, has the right to object to my hon. friend's interfering with anything concerning that constituency. That is what we resent in Nova Scotia. We feel just as keenly about this matter or more so than does the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg. What I say is that we are looking after this matter. Of course the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg comes here and says he represents labour. Who told him that he represented labour, except the labourers in the constituency which he represents? I represent as many labourers as he does, and if they earned the wages that some of the miners in Cape Breton earned they would have ten or twenty thousand dollars in the bank and homes of their own. I have fishermen and lumbermen in my county who work only six months in the year, yet who own their own homes, have money in the bank and are comfortable. So I say it is all nonsense to talk about Besco being wholly to blame for the present condition of affairs, because the miners are to some extent to blame for it themselves. The hon. member for Southeast Grey said last night that these people could not get out of Glace Bay and Sydney. Does she know that 50 per cent of the miners in Cape Breton are unmarried, bachelors? I am surprised that she did not stay down there. She tried to say that these people could not get away from Cape Breton. If anybody else in this country gets out of work, be he a lumberman, a fisherman or anything else, whether he lives in Alberta or any other part of the country, he soon hunts for work somewhere else. Let me also tell the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg that these young bachelors earned anywhere from $90 to $100 in one single week in the month of February. This condition spoken of by the member for Southeast Grey does not exist all over the coal mining area,

but in some of the coal mines they worked 234 days last year. Now working 234 days in a year, at wages of from $3.50 to $6 a day, it seems to me they should not be in the condition in which they were represented to be by the hon. member for Southeast Grey and the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Does the hon. member not know very well that these are not the people who are asking for relief? Some of the miners draw big pay, it is true. They are not on the relief lists at the different stations.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: My hon. friend perhaps was not here when I said there w'ere twenty families the heads of which had $5,000 in the Royal Bank in Glace Bay, who were lined up every day at the soup kitchens and the relief stations.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I doubt it very much.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Of course you do. You were in the charge of the truant officer when you were there. You were in bad company when you were with the mayor of Glace Bay, who for political purposes-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Order. The hon. member must address the Chair.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have another lady who is very much worked up about the distress in Cape Breton, a lady by the name of Mrs. Charles Archibald. I think she is vice-president of the Tory organization in the city of Halifax, and this Mrs. Archibald has been worked up into a great state over the things Premier Armstrong and his government are not doing for these poor distressed people in Cape Breton. This lady is the wife of a gentleman who was manager of a mine in Cape Breton some few years ago known as Port Morien, and now Cow Bay. This Mr. Archibald closed down this mine in the winter of 1894, although the poor miners pleaded with him to keep it open until spring. He closed it down and from seven to eight hundred miners were thrown on the street, and now, of course, Mrs. Archibald, when she has no responsibility, can come along and say: Mr. Armstrong, you and your government must come to the relief of these poor people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I want to ask the hon. gentleman if he is aware that ten thousand people are being fed from Glace Bay proper every day, that ten thousand) people are getting their rations three times a week from the relief station there.

The Budget-Mr. Duff

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
More shame for the mayor of Glace Bay when the British Empire Steel Corporation are assessed 70 per cent, and he could raise the money to feed these people in their homes. Then they would not have to go to relief kitchens or anywhere else.
Mr. Speaker, there is perhaps nothing else I can add. There is no question that it is a serious situation that exists in Cape Breton. My only purpose in rising was to protect the good name of Nova Scotia. As far as the coal situation in Cape Breton is concerned, I am not prejudiced in any way. I have no coal mines in my district, but we are vitally interested in the progress of Cape Breton and in the other counties west, to which we sell a -great deal of goods. In addition to that, we benefit from the royalties which the provincial government collects from the -mines in Cape Breton, and Cumberland and other places. There is no distress around the mining districts of Pictou and Cumberland. There are poor people there, due to the strike, of course, but the difference between the -mayor of Glace Bay and the mayor of New Waterford, and the mayors of Trenton, Stellarton, Westville, New Glasgow and other places, is that they have a proper love of humanity in their hearts, and they are not trying to get elected at the next election.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Might I ask if the
hon. gentleman has not read the appeal that has come from Springhill in the last day or two?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
It is quite possible that somebody in Springhill may be sending in an appeal, like they do in Glace Bay, somebody who is not responsible and 'has no business to do it. But I say the people of Springhill and these districts can look after their own poor. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I am not at all prejudiced. My only interest in discussing this matter is to see that the good name of Nova Scotia is upheld, and until such time as every resource has been exhausted in these cities and towns, which can be assessed for the purpose of looking after these poor people, I say there is no need to -appeal to this government or to the provincial -government. If the mayor and council of Glace Bay should come to this parliament or to the provincial legislature and say: We have exhausted our resources, we have raised every cent we could to look after our poor;-then I say it is time, after the United Mine Workers have sent back the two and a half million dollars, for anybody in this House or in the provincial legislature to say that this government or the provincial government should vote any sum
for the relief of this state of affairs in the county of Cape Breton.
